_note: Red Flags library — fully interactive (severity filter, search, recursive click-through decision tree with correct/incorrect paths highlighted). Seeded with 3 worked scenarios: one drawn directly from the research docs (flag-weather-delay) and two built from the same docs' 'common mistakes' research (flag-small-defect-spiral, flag-silent-problem). Add more toward the 15-20 goal by following the same decisionTree shape: each node is either a branch ({prompt, yes, no}) or a leaf ({action, consequence, nextStep, path: 'correct'|'incorrect'}).

flags.title: Unexpected Weather Threatens Tomorrow's Pour
flags.scenario: Concrete pour is scheduled for tomorrow; the forecast now shows rain moving in with about 48 hours' notice.

decisionTree.prompt: Has the Superintendent confirmed a weather contingency plan?

yes.action: Verify crew notification and confirm the backup date has been communicated to everyone affected.
yes.consequence: You're prepared if the weather hits — no surprises for the crew or the schedule.
yes.nextStep: Monitor weather updates and stay ready to execute the plan.

no.prompt: Do you escalate to the Superintendent immediately?

yes.action: Escalate to the Super immediately; discuss options — delay, cover, or proceed and test.
yes.consequence: Owner, architect, and trades can agree on a decision proactively, before the pour happens.
yes.nextStep: Await the decision and execute once confirmed.

no.action: You proceed without raising it, assuming it'll probably work out.
no.consequence: The pour happens without a contingency in place. If rain hits mid-pour or right after, concrete quality is compromised and the crew wasn't set up with cover.
no.nextStep: This is the mistake: it becomes $50K+ in testing and possible rework — all avoidable with a 5-minute conversation 48 hours earlier.

flags.lesson: Small weather decisions compound. Surface them 48+ hours early, not the morning of.
flags.costOfMissing: $50K+ in testing and potential rework if concrete quality is compromised.
flags.prevention: Daily 48-hour weather check-in with the Super — treat it as a non-negotiable task, not an afterthought.
flags.realExample: This exact failure mode — a known forecast that nobody formally addressed until it was too late — is one of the most common and most preventable causes of concrete quality disputes.

flags.title: A Small Framing Deviation Looks Minor
flags.scenario: During a routine walk you notice wall framing is off-spec by about half an inch. It doesn't look urgent, and three other trades are waiting to build off that wall.

decisionTree.prompt: Could this deviation compound as other trades build off this wall (MEP, drywall, finishes)?

yes.action: Document with a photo and measurement, and notify the Super the same day — even though it looks minor.
yes.consequence: Caught before downstream trades build off a bad reference; costs almost nothing to fix now.
yes.nextStep: Re-inspect after correction before the next trade starts in that area.

no.prompt: Do you document it anyway, just to be safe?

yes.action: Log it as a low-priority punch item and move on.
yes.consequence: Reasonable — it's genuinely isolated and non-structural, and now there's a record either way.
yes.nextStep: Confirm it's closed out before the final walk.

no.action: You let it go unrecorded because it 'looked fine.'
no.consequence: Weeks later it resurfaces during closeout with no documentation trail, and nobody remembers who was responsible for the fix or whether it was ever addressed.
no.nextStep: This is the mistake: undocumented 'minor' issues become disputed issues.

flags.lesson: Small details compound quietly — the ones you don't document are the ones that come back to bite you.
flags.costOfMissing: Rework discovered at closeout costs far more, in dispute time and schedule, than the fix would have during the original walk.
flags.prevention: Document every deviation you notice, however small. A photo and a one-line note costs 30 seconds.
flags.realExample: This is one of the most common defect-tracking gaps regardless of project size — small deviations without documentation are a leading source of 'who approved this' disputes at closeout.

flags.title: You Spot a Coordination Conflict, But Aren't Sure It's Your Job to Raise It
flags.scenario: During a walk you notice electrical rough-in conflicts with an HVAC chase in one room. Nobody's mentioned it yet, and both trades are actively working.

decisionTree.prompt: Will this block or force rework for a trade if it isn't raised now?

yes.action: Raise it the same day: photo, location, both trades' foremen, and the Super — in writing.
yes.consequence: Both trades can resequence before more of either system gets installed in that space.
yes.nextStep: Confirm a resolution plan and re-check before either trade proceeds further in that room.

no.prompt: Are you sure, or just assuming someone else already saw it?

yes.action: Note it in your daily report for the record — no escalation needed.
yes.consequence: Appropriately scaled response for a genuinely non-blocking observation.
yes.nextStep: Keep monitoring as both trades progress.

no.action: You assume someone else will probably catch it and say nothing.
no.consequence: Both trades keep installing in the same space. By the time it's obvious, ripping out and resequencing costs far more than a same-day flag would have.
no.nextStep: This is the mistake: 'someone else probably saw it' is not a plan.

flags.lesson: If you're not sure whether someone else already flagged a conflict, that uncertainty itself is the signal to say something.
flags.costOfMissing: MEP rework after both systems are partially installed is one of the most expensive categories of rework on a job.
flags.prevention: Default to raising anything you notice in writing, even if you assume someone else probably already has — a duplicate flag costs nothing; a missed one costs weeks.
flags.realExample: Different trades genuinely do not talk to each other unless someone makes them — this pattern shows up on almost every MEP-intensive project at some point.
